opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the most interesting things you learn once you're actually serving models at real scale, rather than just benchmarking kernels in isolation.

The two kinds of workloads have very different profiles. Interactive queries, like a chat session or a coding assistant, are latency-sensitive. What users feel is time to first token and then tokens per second after that. So you can't batch too aggressively, because a bigger batch raises per-request latency. Batch workloads, like synthetic data generation, evals, or offline document processing, mostly care about throughput and cost per token. There you want to pack the GPU as full as possible, use large batch sizes, and keep it compute-bound instead of memory-bandwidth-bound.

Running at scale helps because demand for interactive traffic is bursty and follows daily cycles. If you only served interactive traffic, you'd have to provision for peak and then sit with a lot of idle capacity overnight or between bursts. Once you have a big pool of batch work, you can treat it almost like a filler: it soaks up the slack. When interactive demand spikes, you preempt or deprioritize the batch jobs. When it drops, batch fills the gap. Your utilization goes way up, and that's really where the economics of inference come from.

There's also a systems side to this. Things like continuous batching, chunked prefill, and separating prefill from decode all give you more knobs. Prefill is compute-heavy and decode is memory-bound. So at scale you can be smarter about which hardware handles which phase, and how you mix requests so that you're not wasting either compute or bandwidth.

And I think scale gives you data. You see the actual distribution of sequence lengths, how often prefixes get reused, and when the peaks hit. That tells you where to invest. It's things like prefix caching, or which kernels to optimize. It also shows you whether something like speculative decoding pays off for your traffic mix. A lot of the work I've done, on things like FlashAttention, came from looking at where the bottlenecks really are. Serving at scale makes those bottlenecks very concrete.

So the short answer is that scale lets you smooth out demand and push utilization up. It also teaches you exactly where the remaining inefficiencies are, and that feeds back into both the scheduling and the low-level optimization.

r001.rationale: The response says batch work fills spare capacity when interactive demand drops, and can be preempted or deprioritized when interactive demand spikes.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because once you're actually serving models at scale, you realize the two workloads want very different things from the hardware.

Interactive queries are latency-bound. Someone's sitting there watching tokens come out, so you care about time to first token and the per-token decode speed. And decode is fundamentally memory-bandwidth-bound: at small batch sizes you're reading the entire weight matrix and the KV cache for every single token you generate, and the arithmetic units are mostly idle. You're nowhere near the FLOP roofline.

Batch workloads are the opposite. If you're doing offline evaluation, synthetic data generation, or processing a million documents overnight, nobody cares whether an individual request takes two seconds or two minutes. What you care about is throughput per dollar. So you want huge batches, you want the GPU compute-saturated, and you're happy to trade latency for utilization.

The nice thing is that these two are complementary. The interactive traffic leaves the FLOPs on the table, and the batch traffic is exactly what fills them. So the way I think about allocation isn't really "give these GPUs to interactive and these to batch." It's more about scheduling: you reserve enough headroom to hit your latency SLOs for the interactive requests, and then you backfill the remaining capacity with batch work. Interactive traffic is also very bursty, diurnal and so on, so the batch queue becomes this sponge that absorbs the slack.

And a lot of the kernel and systems work connects directly to this. Things like continuous batching, paged KV cache, chunked prefill, speculative decoding: these are all ways to either pull decode closer to the compute roofline or to let you interleave prefill-heavy and decode-heavy requests without one stalling the other. If you can make decode more efficient at moderate batch sizes, you effectively shrink the amount of hardware you need to pin for interactive, and that frees up more for batch.

The other thing that running at scale teaches you is where the actual bottlenecks are, as opposed to where you assumed they were. It's often not the matmuls. It's KV cache memory, it's communication across GPUs, it's the scheduler. And having real traffic to look at tells you which of those is worth optimizing next. So in a sense inference at scale isn't just a consumer of these techniques, it's what tells you which techniques to build.

r001.rationale: The response says to reserve enough capacity for interactive latency targets and backfill remaining capacity with batch work, which absorbs slack when interactive traffic is low.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that interactive queries and batch workloads have different constraints. For an interactive query, you care about how quickly the first token arrives and how quickly you generate subsequent tokens. For a batch job, you mostly care about total throughput and finishing within some deadline.

At scale, you have more flexibility to balance those. You can reserve enough capacity to keep interactive latency low, then use spare capacity for batch work. When interactive demand goes up, you pull back on the batch jobs; when it goes down, you can run larger batches and use the hardware more efficiently.

But you have to be careful: putting more requests together can improve throughput while making individual requests slower. So the goal isn't just maximum GPU utilization. It's maximizing useful work while meeting the latency requirements of each workload.

r001.rationale: The response says spare capacity can serve batch work when interactive demand is low, and batch jobs can be pulled back when interactive demand rises.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that, at scale, you have a mix of workloads with different latency requirements. For an interactive query, you care about how quickly the first token arrives and how quickly subsequent tokens arrive. For a batch workload, you might be happy to get the result hours later, so you can optimize much more aggressively for throughput.

That gives you some flexibility in how you allocate compute. You reserve enough capacity to meet the interactive latency target, and you use the remaining capacity for batch work. When interactive traffic drops, you can run larger batches and get better utilization. When it spikes, you give that traffic priority.

The tricky part is that these workloads share resources, especially GPU memory and memory bandwidth. So it’s not just a matter of filling every idle slot. You want to maximize useful throughput while making sure the batch jobs don’t hurt the latency of the interactive requests.

r001.rationale: It says remaining capacity can serve batch work and that when interactive traffic drops, larger batches can run for better utilization.
